opus-5.5.text:
I think the key insight is that the two aren't really separate problems anymore. If you look at what modern reinforcement learning for large language models actually does, the overwhelming majority of the compute and wall-clock time goes into rollouts, which means generating samples from the policy model. That is inference. So when people talk about building RL infrastructure, a huge part of what they're really asking for is a very fast, very flexible inference engine sitting inside a training loop.

Because of that, a lot of the work we've already done on the inference side carries over directly: efficient batching, KV cache management, prefix sharing, speculative decoding, and scheduling for long and highly variable output lengths. In RL these problems actually get sharper. You might have one prompt that finishes in a few hundred tokens and another that goes on for tens of thousands, and if your system can't handle that long tail gracefully, your expensive training GPUs just sit idle. So the expertise you build serving models in production is exactly the expertise you need to make RL efficient.

The other reason it feels manageable is that the interface between the two is relatively clean. The training framework needs to push updated weights to the inference engine, the inference engine needs to return trajectories, and you need to coordinate memory and placement, whether you're co-locating them on the same GPUs or splitting them across separate pools. Those are real engineering challenges, such as weight synchronization, numerical consistency between training and inference, and handling agentic multi-turn rollouts with tool calls, but they're well-scoped. You don't have to rebuild the training stack from scratch. You can integrate with existing training frameworks and focus on making the rollout side excellent.

And honestly, working on both together makes each one better. RL users push the inference engine in directions that normal serving workloads don't, and those improvements then flow back to everyone serving models in production. So rather than doubling the scope, it's more like the same core system serving two communities, with a lot of shared benefit.

r001.rationale: The response identifies rollouts as a major source of RL compute and difficulty, but does not identify the reward engine as difficult.

r002.rationale: It calls rollout generation inference, but does not describe the reward engine as an inference engine.

r003.rationale: It says RL infrastructure relies heavily on the same inference capabilities and systems work, including batching, KV cache management, scheduling, and weight coordination.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key insight is that they're not really two separate systems once you look at where the time actually goes. In a modern RL loop for language models, the rollout phase, where the policy generates samples, is just inference. And it usually dominates the wall-clock time. So if you've already built a serious inference engine, with good batching, KV cache management, prefix sharing, and so on, you've already solved most of the hard part of RL infrastructure. The training step is comparatively well understood.

That's how I see it from the SGLang side. We built SGLang first as a serving system, and then the RL use case showed up almost naturally. The rollout workloads actually benefit from the same things production serving benefits from. Many samples from the same prompt share a prefix, so RadixAttention helps. You need high throughput over latency, so continuous batching matters. Those weren't new features we had to invent for RL; they were already there.

The genuinely new pieces for RL are narrower than people expect. The main ones are weight synchronization, so the inference engine can pick up updated policy weights quickly without restarting, and then the scheduling question of how to overlap generation with training so the GPUs aren't sitting idle. Those are real engineering problems, but they're bounded. You can scope them, build them, and test them, rather than redesigning the whole stack.

The other reason I think it's manageable is organizational. Having one team own both means when something is slow, you don't have the inference people and the RL people pointing at each other. The same people who know how the KV cache behaves are the ones figuring out why rollouts stall. That shortens the debugging loop a lot.

So I wouldn't say it's easy. But the overlap is large enough that doing them together is actually less work than building two separate systems that then have to be glued together.

r001.rationale: The response discusses rollout generation, weight synchronization, and scheduling as RL engineering concerns, but does not identify a reward engine as a major source of difficulty.

r002.rationale: It describes the rollout phase as inference, but does not identify the reward engine as an inference engine.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says inference and RL infrastructure share much of the same work, including batching and KV cache management, and that their overlap makes a combined system manageable.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s manageable because there’s a lot of overlap between the two. In reinforcement learning, you generate responses, evaluate them, and then use that feedback to update the model. That generation step is inference, so an efficient inference engine is already a major building block for reinforcement learning infrastructure.

Of course, reinforcement learning adds requirements: you need to coordinate generation with training, update model weights, and manage resources across those stages. So they’re not identical systems. But you can build on shared foundations, with additional orchestration for the reinforcement learning loop, rather than developing two entirely separate stacks.

r001.rationale: The response mentions added RL requirements and orchestration, but does not identify the reward engine as a major source of difficulty.

r002.rationale: It identifies the response-generation step as inference, but does not identify the reward engine itself as an inference engine.

r003.rationale: It says the systems have “a lot of overlap,” share foundations, and can build on the same inference engine.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s manageable because the two share a lot of the same underlying infrastructure. In reinforcement learning, you generate outputs from the model, evaluate them, and then use that feedback to update the model. That generation step is inference, so improvements in inference efficiency also help reinforcement learning.

There are additional challenges, like coordinating rollout workers with training workers and keeping model weights up to date. But you’re building on a common foundation. If you keep the interfaces clear, you can reuse much of the system while handling those differences in separate components.

r001.rationale: The response mentions evaluating model outputs and feedback, but does not identify the reward engine as a major source of difficulty.

r002.rationale: It calls the output-generation step inference, but does not identify the reinforcement learning reward engine itself as an inference engine.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says the two share much of the same underlying infrastructure and that much of the system can be reused.
